item.title: Hydraulic tests completed at Turkey's Akkuyu 1
item.description: Hydraulic tests to check the primary circuit systems and equipment at unit 1 of Turkey's Akkuyu nuclear power plant have been successfully completed, paving the way for hot functional tests to begin.
item.wnn:fullText:
During the tests, the pressure in the primary circuit (the reactor, main circulation pumps, steam generators, the pressuriser, and the main circulation pipeline connecting them) was increased to 24.5 MPa - about one-and-a-half times higher than the reactor's normal operating pressure. The temperature of the primary circuit water at the initial stage of the operation reached 135°C. Specialists checked equipment status to ensure everything was in line with design requirements and international safety standards. An automated process control system (APCS) was put into operation during the hydraulic tests.

To conduct the hydraulic tests, the primary circuit was filled with chemically demineralised water, after which the required pressure and temperature were created using the main circulation pump units. During the tests, the unit's operating personnel in the control room monitored the condition of the equipment and pipelines using data from the APCS.


(Image: Rosatom)

During normal operation of the power unit, coolant - demineralised water at a temperature of up to 330°C under a pressure of about 16 MPa - circulates through the primary circuit, heating the secondary circuit feedwater in the steam generators.

Cold hydraulic tests, which began in June following the loading of dummy fuel, are carried out to confirm whether components and systems important to safety are properly installed and ready to operate in a cold condition. The main purpose of cold functional tests is to verify the leak-tightness of the primary circuit and components and to clean the main circulation pipes. The tests mark the first time the reactor systems are operated together with the auxiliary systems.

These are followed by the hot functional tests to confirm that equipment and systems are ready for operating conditions, including checking the operation of the four main circulation pumps at temperatures of at least 260°C. Both cold and hot tests take place before the loading of nuclear fuel in the commissioning process.

"During the construction of unit 1 of the Akkuyu NPP, thousands of complex engineering operations were completed," said Alexey Likhachev, Director General of Rosatom. "We are now at the stage where the results of this enormous undertaking are undergoing a comprehensive review. The safe operation of the entire unit depends on the reliability of the primary circuit. Exceptionally high technological requirements are placed on the equipment, pipelines, and welded joints here. Hydraulic testing has been successfully completed. This is convincing confirmation of the quality of the installation, welding, and commissioning work - and another step towards the unit's physical startup."

Background

Akkuyu, in the southern Mersin province, is Turkey's first nuclear power plant. Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom is building four VVER-1200 reactors, under a so-called BOO (build-own-operate) model. According to the terms of the 2010 Intergovernmental Agreement between the Russian Federation and the Republic of Turkey, the aim was for the commissioning of the first power unit of the nuclear power plant to take place within seven years from receipt of all permits for the construction of the unit.


(Image: Rosatom)

The licence for the construction of the first unit was issued in 2018, with construction work beginning that year. Nuclear fuel was delivered to the site in April 2023. The aim has been for unit 1 to begin supplying Turkey's energy system by the end of 2026.

When the 4,800 MWe plant is completed, it is expected to meet about 10% of Turkey's electricity needs.

Turkey has plans for a second nuclear power plant, at Sinop, and has also been in talks with China about plans for a third plant, in the Thrace region in the country's north-west.

The country is also developing plans for small modular reactors, with the aim of adding 5 GWe of capacity by 2050 - which would mean the equivalent of at least 16 individual SMRs.

item.title: Bangladesh's Rooppur 1 achieves criticality
item.description: The first unit at Bangladesh's Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant achieved criticality - a self-sustaining nuclear reaction - at 15:34 on Sunday, 11 October.
item.wnn:fullText:
The milestone was achieved three days after the go-ahead was given by the country's national atomic regulator.

A statement on the project's official Facebook account said: "This achievement is a significant step in Bangladesh's scientific and technological advancements and in the country's energy security. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant will play a crucial role in strengthening the country's energy security, diversifying electricity generation, and improving the development of low-carbon fuel systems.

"After achieving the required criteria, the test and safety verification process will be completed, and the reactor will be tested to operate at the minimum controllable capacity. If the subsequent tests are successfully completed, the national grid power supply operations will be advanced step by step."

The start-up of the unit followed talks in Moscow on Friday between Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev and Bangladesh's Science and Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam.

Likhachev said: "Reaching the minimum control level is a significant milestone in the implementation of the Rooppur NPP unit 1 project and a major achievement for the entire project team. Upon successful completion of this phase, the unit will be ready for the power start-up phase and subsequent connection to the Bangladesh power grid."


(Image: Rosatom)

According to Strana Rosatom, the in-house publication of Russia’s state nuclear corporation, the power start-up of the unit is scheduled for 20 November.

Before then there will be a series of tests and checks to ensure that all equipment and systems are working as designed. There will then be further tests and checks before the power start-up and as the power output is subsequently increased in stages.

Criticality means that the reactor has achieved a sustained nuclear chain reaction, with each fission event - when an atom of uranium in the fuel is split - releasing a sufficient number of neutrons to sustain an ongoing series of reactions.

Background

In February 2011 Russia's Rosatom signed an agreement for two reactors to be built at Rooppur, about 160 kilometres from the capital Dhaka, for the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission. The initial contract for the project, worth USD12.65 billion, was signed in December 2015. The Bangladesh Atomic Regulatory Authority issued the first site licence for the Rooppur plant in June 2016, allowing preliminary site works, including geological surveys, to begin.

Construction of the first unit began in November 2017. Construction of the second unit began in July 2018. They have an initial life-cycle of 60 years, with a further 20-year extension possible.

The first batch of nuclear fuel was delivered to the site in October 2023 - the moment that the site got its status as a nuclear facility. In March last year, Rooppur unit 1's turbine installation was completed, as were hydraulic tests to check the primary circuit systems and equipment, followed by hot functional tests. An operating licence was issued by the Bangladesh Nuclear Regulatory Authority on 16 April this year. The process of loading 163 nuclear fuel assemblies into Bangladesh's first nuclear power plant reactor was completed in May.

Meanwhile, Rosatom announced on Monday 12 October, that JSC Rosatom Automated Control Systems had completed the installation of automated process control systems at the first and second power units of the Rooppur plant. Likhachev said: "The Rooppur NPP is not only the largest project of cooperation between the Russian Federation and the Republic of Bangladesh, but also our flagship in the use of modern automation and control technologies. This is Rosatom's first foreign plant to implement the Operator Information Support System. The system increases response times and reduces operating costs."

item.title: Czech SMR environmental impact assessment submitted
item.description: ČEZ has submitted the Environmental Impact Assessment documentation to the Ministry of the Environment for its Rolls-Royce SMR small modular reactor project in Temelín.
item.wnn:fullText:
The submission of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is a key part of the permitting process and assesses the potential impact on the area from the proposed small modular reactor (SMR) project, as well as putting forward steps to minimise any impact.

ČEZ said: "We pay significant attention to water. Water availability is one of the basic criteria when selecting and preparing locations for SMRs. Preparation includes detailed surveys and long-term monitoring focused, among other things, on water resources and their future availability. The results so far confirm that water availability does not represent an obstacle, even when taking into account the worsening drought."

The ministry will assess the documentation and take public comments. The EIA process is expected to be completed by the end of 2027.

Daniel Beneš, Chairman and CEO of ČEZ, said: "We are counting on small modular reactors alongside large nuclear power plants and renewable sources. They are also a great opportunity for Czech companies. The supply chain for small modular reactors is being formed right now. Companies that join this global chain at the very beginning have the potential to win orders for decades to come, because they will supply the entire SMR fleet in the Czech Republic and abroad."

Background

The Rolls-Royce SMR is a 470 MWe design based on a small pressurised water reactor. It will provide consistent baseload generation for at least 60 years. Ninety percent of the SMR - measuring about 16 metres by 4 metres - will be built in factory conditions, limiting activity on-site primarily to assembly of pre-fabricated, pre-tested, modules which significantly reduces project risk and has the potential to drastically shorten build schedules.

In October 2024, Rolls-Royce SMR was selected by ČEZ to deploy up to 3 GW of electricity in the Czech Republic, and ČEZ took a 20% stake in Rolls-Royce SMR. The plan is for this first SMR to be deployed in the area of the Temelín site (which already has two gigawatt-scale VVER-1000 units), with further projects being developed for coal-fired power plant sites, including Tušimice.

In June 2025, Rolls-Royce SMR was selected as the UK government's preferred technology for the country's first SMR project. In November, the UK government announced that Wylfa on the island of Anglesey, North Wales, would be the site to host the three Rolls-Royce SMR units. It said the site - where a Magnox plant is being decommissioned - could potentially host up to eight SMRs. A final investment decision is expected to be taken in 2029.

The submission of the EIA follows the signing of Early Works Contracts between Rolls-Royce SMR and ČEZ, supporting the preparation of the site and working to secure the permits required for construction at Temelín. It also builds on a memorandum of understanding signed earlier this year between Rolls-Royce SMR, ČEZ and the Czech Ministry of Industry and Trade which enabled site preparation activities for further deployments in Tušimice and Dětmarovice.

The UK project is expected to be the first Rolls-Royce SMR deployed, with Temelín to host the second, with a target operational date "in the second half of the 2030s".

item.title: Agreement signed on second Polish nuclear power plant
item.description: Poland's Ministry of Energy, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe and Polska Grupa Energetyczna have signed an agreement defining the division of tasks and principles of cooperation in preparing the construction of the country's second nuclear power plant.
item.wnn:fullText:
In September 2021, it was announced that six large pressurised water reactors with a combined installed capacity of 6-9 GWe could be built by 2040 as part of the country's plan to reduce its reliance on coal. According to the adopted schedule, the construction of the first nuclear power plant would start in 2026, with the first reactor - with a capacity of 1.0-1.6 GWe - being commissioned in 2033. Subsequent units would be implemented every 2 to 3 years.

The Lubiatowo-Kopalino site in the Choczewo municipality in Pomerania in northern Poland was selected as the preferred location for the country's first large nuclear power plant, which will have a capacity of 3,750 MWe, using Westinghouse's AP1000 technology. An agreement setting a plan for the delivery of the plant was signed in May 2023 by Westinghouse, Bechtel and Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ). Construction is scheduled to begin in 2028.

Work has now started on the second nuclear power plant, with Bełchatów and Konin the preferred locations.

PEJ - a special-purpose vehicle 100% owned by Poland's State Treasury - is to be the investor and coordinator of the second nuclear power plant project, while state-owned power company Polska Grupa Energetyczna (PGE) will prepare site analyses and preliminary feasibility studies in collaboration with potential technology suppliers, according to a new agreement signed by the Ministry of Energy, PEJ and PGE. The document introduces the assumptions of the updated Polish nuclear power programme, adopted by the Council of Ministers on 29 September.

"The cooperation is intended to ensure the effective use of the resources and experience of both companies and to improve investment preparation, also through appropriate coordination of activities at the government administration level," the Ministry of Energy said. It noted that PEJ was responsible for preparing the design of the first Polish nuclear power plant, while PGE - whose group includes PGE Energia Jądrowa - also has experience in preparing nuclear projects.

Under the recent update to the country's nuclear power programme, the first unit is now scheduled to start commercial operation in 2036, and the plant is expected to reach full capacity by 2038 - three years later than previously planned.

The ministry said a competitive dialogue was under way to select a technology supplier and project contractor for the second plant. The USA, France, and Canada have joined the process. "A key element of this process will be for suppliers to prepare preliminary feasibility studies for power plants using the technologies they offer," it said. "The aim of the procedure is to select a comprehensive offer encompassing technology, investment financing, and elements of broader strategic cooperation. For the second power plant, as for the first, the proven technology of large-scale Generation III+ light-water reactors is being considered."

Key milestones for the second power plant under the updated nuclear power programme are: the selection of a strategic partner and technology in 2027; construction to start around 2032; and the first unit to start up around 2040 – one year behind the previous schedule.

The ministry said the final decision on the second plant would be made after conducting the necessary research and analyses to confirm the feasibility of the investment.

Agreement welcomed

"The construction of a second nuclear power plant is an undertaking that requires close cooperation between the state and state-owned companies," said Minister of State Assets Wojciech Balczun. "Today's agreement demonstrates our exemplary cooperation, effectively combining the expertise and experience of various entities to achieve the common goal of Poland's energy security."

Wojciech Wrochna, Deputy Minister of Energy and Government Plenipotentiary for Strategic Energy Infrastructure, added: "We now have site analyses, feasibility studies, and technology selection ahead of us. We intend to conduct this process competitively to develop favourable investment implementation conditions, taking into account not only technology but also financing and long-term strategic cooperation."

"We are embarking on the second nuclear power plant with something we didn't have at the start of the first investment: experience from the first project," said Marek Woszczyk, President of the Management Board of PEJ. "We know how to manage administrative processes, organise dialogue with partners, and prepare for implementation of a project of this scale."

Dariusz Lubera, President of the Management Board of PGE, said: "I believe that the combination of knowledge, experience, and competence of both companies will enable the successful implementation of this ambitious project, which is of strategic importance for the future of the Polish energy sector and the entire economy."

item.title: Hot testing of Chinese SMR under way
item.description: Tests that simulate the temperatures and pressures which the reactor systems will be subjected to during normal operation are reportedly taking place at the ACP100 small modular reactor demonstration project, under construction at the Changjiang site on China's island province of Hainan.
item.wnn:fullText:
Hot functional tests involve increasing the temperature of the reactor coolant system and carrying out comprehensive tests to ensure that coolant circuits and safety systems are operating as they should. Carried out before the loading of nuclear fuel, such testing simulates the thermal working conditions of the power plant and verifies that nuclear island and conventional equipment and systems meet design requirements.

A report from the official China News Service says these tests are now under way at the ACP100 - also referred to as the Linglong One - with the aim of loading fuel into the reactor within the year.

Background

China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) announced in July 2019 the launch of a project to construct an ACP100 SMR at Changjiang. The site is already home to two operating CNP600 pressurised water reactors (PWRs), while the construction of two Hualong One units began in March and December 2021. The first of these Hualong One units entered commercial operation last month, with the second scheduled to follow early next year.

First concrete for the ACP100 was poured on 13 July 2021, with a planned total construction period of 58 months. Equipment installation work commenced in December 2022 and the main internal structure of the reactor building was completed in March 2023. The outer containment dome was hoisted into place in February last year.

Cold functional tests - carried out to confirm whether components and systems important to safety are properly installed and ready to operate in cold conditions - were completed in October last year. The main purpose of those tests was to verify the leak-tightness of the primary circuit and components - such as pressure vessels, pipelines and valves of both the nuclear and conventional islands - and to clean the main circulation pipes. The tests mark the first time the reactor systems were operated together with the auxiliary systems.

Under development since 2010, the 125 MWe ACP100 integrated PWR's preliminary design was completed in 2014. In 2016, the design became the first SMR to pass a safety review by the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Once completed, the Changjiang ACP100 reactor will be capable of producing 1 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, enough to meet the needs of 526,000 households. The reactor is designed for electricity production, heating, steam production or seawater desalination.

item.title: Westinghouse places initial orders for Polish plant
item.description: Westinghouse has placed conditional purchase orders for safety-related modules with four Polish companies, a week after being commissioned to begin ordering long-lead items for the first unit of Poland's planned first nuclear power plant.
item.wnn:fullText:
Three Westinghouse AP1000 reactors are planned for the plant at the Lubiatowo-Kopalino site in the Choczewo municipality in Pomerania in northern Poland. The AP1000 reactor design uses modular construction techniques, enabling large structural modules to be built at factories and then installed at the site. The reactor building and systems consist of dozens of prefabricated, steel-concrete structural and mechanical modules.

Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) last week gave Westinghouse the go-ahead to start ordering long-lead items for the project's first AP1000 unit. It said the scope of the order for the first unit covers six key components of the nuclear island, including the reactor containment vessel and associated structural modules.

Westinghouse has now placed conditional purchase orders with Energomontaż-Północ Gdynia SA (EPG), FAMAK SA, Mostostal Kielce SA and Mostostal Krakow SA to support the first AP1000 unit at the Lubiatowo-Kopalino site.

The conditional purchase orders cover the CA02 Walls Module Scope for Mostostal Kielce, the CA03 Module Scope for EPG, the CA05 Walls Module Scope for Mostostal Krakow, and the CA20 Floors Module Scope for FAMAK.

In an AP1000 unit, the CA02 walls module and the CA03 module are part of the in-containment refuelling water storage tank in the containment building. The CA05 walls module consists of reinforced steel plates that provide protective walls separating various rooms in the containment building. The CA20 floors module consists of reinforced concrete slabs placed on steel plates to form the floors of the larger CA20 module that houses plant equipment inside the unit.

Westinghouse said that, as part of its ongoing supplier development programme, each of the four companies is steadily progressing toward full NQA-1 compliance. Upon NQA-1 certification and the successful fabrication of pre-production qualification mock-ups - which demonstrate increasing readiness to support future nuclear safety-related manufacturing activities - Westinghouse will award companies the full project scope.

"Westinghouse has been very impressed with the technical capabilities of Polish industry and the potential for these local suppliers in making an immediate impact in the project," said Dan Lipman, President of Global Business Initiatives at Westinghouse. "Working closely with our customer, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe, we have established partnerships with Polish companies to manufacture and supply safety-related modules for Unit 1 of Poland's first AP1000 nuclear power plant. These local suppliers will not only help us deliver the project on time and on budget, but they will also gain valuable experience that will give them an opportunity to participate in additional AP1000 projects in Poland, across Europe and around the world."

Marek Woszczyk, President of the Management Board of PEJ, added: "These conditional purchase orders are tangible proof that Polish companies are moving closer to contributing to the construction of Poland's first nuclear power plant. The progress made by EPG, FAMAK, Mostostal Kielce and Mostostal Krakow in meeting NQA-1 requirements demonstrates both the strength of Polish industry and its potential to become part of the global AP1000 supply chain, supporting not only our project but also future AP1000 projects worldwide."

Early procurement of components with long lead times is common in nuclear projects worldwide. It helps secure the availability of production capacity, mitigates the risk of delays, and supports timely project implementation. The scope of work includes preparing technical documentation, quality and supervision plans, selecting and contracting suppliers, and initiating material procurement necessary to commence production. The production and delivery of finished components to the construction site will be handled as part of a subsequent order, which PEJ plans to issue as part of the power plant construction contract.

Last month, Polish construction engineering firm Polimex Mostostal was selected by Bechtel to deliver, assemble and commission two large-scale assembly halls as part of the project to construct the Lubiatowo-Kopalino plant. Under the contract, Polimex Mostostal will provide a key element of the production and assembly facilities for the construction of three Westinghouse AP1000 units commissioned by PEJ. The contract includes a full range of engineering services, including the development of design documentation for obtaining necessary permits, as well as the supply of materials, structural assembly, testing, acceptance, and final handover of both halls.

Construction of the Lubiatowo-Kopalino plant is scheduled to begin in 2028. Under the recent update to the country's nuclear power programme, the first unit is scheduled to start commercial operation in 2036, and the plant is expected to reach full capacity by 2038 - three years later than previously planned.

item.title: Joint venture formed for six-unit SMR plant in Poland
item.description: Poland's SGE and ZE Pak have agreed to establish a joint venture to develop a nuclear power plant in Pątnów which will feature up to six BWRX-300 small modular reactors.
item.wnn:fullText:
SGE (previously Sythos Green Energy) has a number of potential projects under way across Europe - including in Poland, where a decision in principle has already been issued for a total of 26 BWRX-300 small modular reactors (SMRs), and in the UK where a proposal for a fleet of 14 of the SMRs across three sites is being considered under the UK's Advanced Nuclear Framework programme.

It is a co-investor in the standard design of GE Vernova Hitachi's BWRX-300. The proposed plant with six of the SMRs would have a capacity of 1,800 MWe.

The planned SGE–ZE PAK project will repurpose an existing coal plant, which is owned by ZE PAK, who said its "participation will consist of contributing rights to land currently owned by the company to the joint venture. In subsequent years, ZE PAK will have the option to remain in the project as a minority shareholder or sell its shares in the company managing the project to SGE, thus ending its involvement in the project".

Michał Sołowow, founder of SGE, said: "Today's agreement between SGE and ZE PAK lays a strong foundation for deploying six safe and efficient BWRX-300 reactors at Pątnów. This is one of the most strategically important locations in Poland's energy system. The existing coal-fired power plant will inevitably have to shut down, and without a reliable replacement, its closure could disrupt grid operations. Replacing coal-fired generation with nuclear power based on SMR technology will bring Poland's energy system into the 21st century."

Piotr Żak, President of ZE PAK, said: "This agreement represents a major opportunity for the Konin area and its residents. Building a nuclear power plant on the site of our former coal operations would be a model example of Poland’s energy transition. The energy and fuel crises of recent years have made one thing clear: Poland needs reliable, domestic sources of electricity. The six SMR reactors planned for the ZE PAK site can provide exactly that."

ZE PAK said that "recent experience has shown that the construction of large-scale nuclear reactors should be a state-owned enterprise, while SMR technology can be developed by private entities such as SGE".

The first BWRX-300 is currently under construction in Canada, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has issued a construction permit for the first BWRX-300 reactor at the Clinch River site in Tennessee, and the SMR has also been selected for projects being developed by SaskPower in Canada, Blue Energy in the USA, and Studsvik in Sweden.

item.title: US DOE funding to accelerate molten salt reactor development
item.description: The Molten Chloride Reactor Experiment aims to achieve first criticality in 2027, with the US Department of Energy approving cost-shared funding under its Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program.
item.wnn:fullText:
The funding for an accelerated final stage is intended to support work by utility Southern Company, Idaho National Laboratory and maritime nuclear specialist Core Power to "advance scientific understanding of molten salt reactor technology and inform future reactor development".

The Molten Chloride Reactor Experiment is expected to generate data on the behaviour of the fuel, reactor operation and performance "providing the scientific and engineering foundation needed to support future reactor design, licensing pathways and commercial deployment".

Jess Gehin, associate laboratory director for Nuclear Science and Technology at Idaho National Laboratory, said: "MCRE (The Molten Chloride Reactor Experiment) will be the world's first fast-spectrum molten chloride reactor to achieve criticality. It will provide direct measurements of how this novel reactor behaves during sustained fission, data that until now, has come from models alone. Enhancing those models with real-world operating evidence will reduce uncertainty for future reactor designers and regulators."

Mark Berry, Southern Company senior vice president of research, environment and sustainability, said: "Public-private partnerships play an essential role in advancing energy technologies from concept to demonstration. Through collaboration among DOE, Idaho National Laboratory and industry partners, MCRE will help expand knowledge of molten salt reactor technology and help reduce technical uncertainty for future developers."

Mikal Bøe, CEO of Core Power, said: "Core Power's role in this partnership is to help translate advanced reactor technology into deployable industrial systems and unique delivery mechanisms needed to realise the potential of this technology. Merging the pathway of novel nuclear fuel cycle development that MCRE represents with Core Power's pathway of maritime nuclear development, creates unique opportunities to deliver an ultimately sustainable nuclear fuel solution to new markets around the world. One such market is a sustainable future of civil maritime nuclear propulsion of large commercial ships, where an enduring, zero-emission power source can transform the way global trade is transported at sea."

The Molten Chloride Reactor Experiment uses liquid salt as the fuel and the coolant, allowing for high operating temperatures to efficiently produce heat or electricity. It will need 72 to 75 batches of fuel salt to enable it to go critical - giving Idaho National Laboratory its largest fuel production challenge in 30 years, according to the DOE Office of Nuclear Energy. The fuel salt production process began in 2020, but early attempts yielded far below the goal of 90% conversion of uranium metal into uranium chloride and production of 18 kg of fuel salt per batch. But a breakthrough in 2024 - when the team developed a new step to improve uranium utilisation - eventually led to the achievement of 95% conversion and full-batch production. They have since demonstrated they can produce a batch in as little as one day, according to INL.
